summary.text: Let \(r\in[1/2,1]\) satisfy \(H(r)=r\log 2\), where \(H\) is binary entropy; bounding each residue by both \(2^k\) and \(\binom nk\), together with \(\log\binom nk\le nH(k/n)\), gives the exponential upper rate \(r\log 2\). For the matching lower bound, choose \(y>r\) arbitrarily close to \(r\): then \(H(y)<y\log 2\), so for \(k=\lfloor yn\rfloor\) the binomial coefficient is eventually unchanged modulo \(2^k\), while a binomial-distribution mode estimate gives \(\log\binom nk\ge nH(k/n)-\log(n+1)\); hence \(\log a(n)/n\to r\log 2\) and the roots tend to \(e^{r\log 2}\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=1}^n \left(\binom nk\bmod 2^k\right),
\]
where each residue is the least nonnegative residue. We prove that the sequence of real numbers \(a(n)^{1/n}\) converges.

Define the binary entropy function (using natural logarithms) by
\[
H(x)=-x\log x-(1-x)\log(1-x),\qquad 0<x<1,
\]
with its continuous endpoint values \(H(0)=H(1)=0\). We shall use the standard facts that \(H\) is continuous on \([0,1]\), that
\[
H(1/2)=\log 2,
\]
and that \(H\) is strictly decreasing on \([1/2,1]\). The last fact also follows directly by differentiation on \((1/2,1)\), since
\[
H'(x)=\log\frac{1-x}{x}<0.
\]

Put
\[
g(x)=H(x)-x\log 2.
\]
At the endpoints of \([1/2,1]\),
\[
g(1/2)=\frac12\log 2>0,
\qquad
g(1)=-\log 2<0.
\]
By continuity there is an \(r\in[1/2,1]\) such that
\[
g(r)=0,
\quad\text{that is,}\quad
H(r)=r\log 2.
\tag{1}
\]
Moreover \(r<1\), because \(g(1)<0\). (In fact this crossing is unique, although uniqueness is not needed.) Set
\[
\lambda=r\log 2=H(r).
\tag{2}
\]
We will prove
\[
\frac{\log a(n)}n\longrightarrow \lambda.
\tag{3}
\]
The desired result will then follow by exponentiation.

We first establish the binomial-coefficient estimates needed in both directions.

Fix integers \(0\le k\le n\), and, when \(n>0\), put \(x=k/n\). The binomial theorem gives
\[
\sum_{j=0}^n \binom nj x^j(1-x)^{n-j}=1.
\tag{4}
\]
Every term in this sum is nonnegative. In particular, its \(j=k\) term is at most 1:
\[
\binom nk\left(\frac kn\right)^k
       \left(\frac{n-k}{n}\right)^{n-k}\le 1.
\tag{5}
\]
If \(0<k<n\), all factors here are positive, so taking logarithms and rearranging yields
\[
\log\binom nk
\le -k\log\frac kn-(n-k)\log\frac{n-k}{n}
=nH(k/n).
\tag{6}
\]
The same inequality is immediate for \(k=0\) and \(k=n\), since then \(\binom nk=1\) and \(H(0)=H(1)=0\). Thus, for every \(0\le k\le n\),
\[
\boxed{\ \log\binom nk\le nH(k/n).\ }
\tag{7}
\]

We will also need a lower estimate. Assume \(0<k<n\), let \(p=k/n\), and define
\[
P_j=\binom nj p^j(1-p)^{n-j}\qquad(0\le j\le n).
\]
These numbers sum to 1 by (4). We claim that \(P_k\) is a largest one among them. Indeed, the usual adjacent-term identity gives
\[
P_{j+1}(j+1)(n-k)=P_j(n-j)k.
\tag{8}
\]
For \(j<k\), one has
\[
(j+1)(n-k)\le (n-j)k,
\]
so (8) implies \(P_j\le P_{j+1}\). For \(k\le j<n\), one has the reverse inequality
\[
(n-j)k\le (j+1)(n-k),
\]
so \(P_{j+1}\le P_j\). Hence the terms increase up to \(k\) and decrease thereafter, proving the claim.

There are \(n+1\) terms in (4), all at most \(P_k\), and their sum is 1. Consequently
\[
1\le(n+1)P_k
=(n+1)\binom nk
  \left(\frac kn\right)^k
  \left(\frac{n-k}{n}\right)^{n-k}.
\]
Taking logarithms and using
\[
nH(k/n)=-k\log(k/n)-(n-k)\log((n-k)/n)
\]
gives
\[
\boxed{\ nH(k/n)-\log(n+1)\le\log\binom nk\ }
\qquad(0<k<n).
\tag{9}
\]
Thus (7) and (9) provide an entropy approximation to \(\log\binom nk\), with an error no larger than \(\log(n+1)\).

We next derive the upper bound for \(a(n)\). For \(0\le k\le n\), write \(x=k/n\) when \(n>0\). We claim that
\[
\binom nk\bmod 2^k\le e^{n\lambda}.
\tag{10}
\]
There are two cases.

First suppose \(x\le r\). A residue modulo \(2^k\) is less than \(2^k\), and hence at most \(2^k\). Since \(k=nx\le nr\),
\[
\binom nk\bmod 2^k
\le 2^k=e^{k\log2}
\le e^{nr\log2}=e^{n\lambda}.
\]

Now suppose \(x\ge r\). Then necessarily \(x\in[1/2,1]\), because \(r\ge1/2\). Since \(H\) decreases on this interval,
\[
H(x)\le H(r)=\lambda.
\]
Also a residue is at most the original integer. By (7),
\[
\binom nk\bmod 2^k
\le\binom nk
\le e^{nH(x)}
\le e^{n\lambda}.
\]
This proves (10) in all cases. There are exactly \(n\) indices in the defining sum for \(a(n)\), so
\[
a(n)\le n e^{n\lambda}.
\tag{11}
\]

Notice also that \(a(n)>0\) whenever \(n>0\): the summand with \(k=n\) equals
\[
\binom nn\bmod 2^n=1\bmod 2^n=1.
\tag{12}
\]
Thus logarithms of \(a(n)\) are legitimate for positive \(n\). Taking logarithms in (11) and dividing by \(n\) gives
\[
\frac{\log a(n)}n\le \lambda+\frac{\log n}{n}.
\]
Since \(\log n/n\to0\), we obtain
\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log a(n)}n\le\lambda.
\tag{13}
\]

It remains to prove the matching lower bound. We will show that for every real number \(b<\lambda\), eventually
\[
b<\frac{\log a(n)}n.
\tag{14}
\]

Fix \(b<\lambda=H(r)\). By continuity of \(H\) at \(r\), and because \(r<1\), we may choose a number \(y\) such that
\[
r<y<1
\quad\text{and}\quad
b<H(y).
\tag{15}
\]
Because \(y>r\ge1/2\) and \(H\) is strictly decreasing on \([1/2,1]\),
\[
H(y)<H(r)=r\log2<y\log2.
\tag{16}
\]
In other words, \(g(y)<0\).

For each \(n\), choose
\[
k_n=\lfloor yn\rfloor,
\qquad x_n=\frac{k_n}{n}.
\]
Since \(0<y<1\), as \(n\to\infty\) we have
\[
x_n\longrightarrow y,
\tag{17}
\]
and eventually \(0<k_n<n\). By continuity of \(H\) and \(g\), equations (15)--(17) imply that, for all sufficiently large \(n\),
\[
b<H(x_n)
\tag{18}
\]
and
\[
g(x_n)=H(x_n)-x_n\log2<0.
\tag{19}
\]
The latter inequality is precisely
\[
nH(x_n)<nx_n\log2=k_n\log2.
\tag{20}
\]
Using the upper entropy estimate (7), we therefore obtain
\[
\log\binom n{k_n}
\le nH(x_n)
<k_n\log2
=\log(2^{k_n}).
\]
Both quantities inside the logarithms are positive, so strict monotonicity of the logarithm gives
\[
\binom n{k_n}<2^{k_n}.
\tag{21}
\]
This is the key reason for choosing a proportion just to the right of the crossing point: at this index the binomial coefficient is already smaller than the modulus. Thus modular reduction does nothing:
\[
\binom n{k_n}\bmod 2^{k_n}=\binom n{k_n}.
\tag{22}
\]
Since eventually \(1\le k_n\le n\), this is one of the nonnegative summands defining \(a(n)\). Therefore
\[
a(n)\ge\binom n{k_n}.
\tag{23}
\]
Applying the lower entropy estimate (9) to \(k_n\), and then (23), gives
\[
\log a(n)
\ge \log\binom n{k_n}
\ge nH(x_n)-\log(n+1).
\]
After division by \(n\),
\[
\frac{\log a(n)}n
\ge H(x_n)-\frac{\log(n+1)}n.
\tag{24}
\]
Now \(H(x_n)\to H(y)\), while
\[
\frac{\log(n+1)}n\longrightarrow0.
\]
Because \(b<H(y)\), (24) is strictly greater than \(b\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). This proves (14). Since (14) holds for every \(b<\lambda\),
\[
\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log a(n)}n\ge\lambda.
\tag{25}
\]
Combining (13) and (25) proves (3):
\[
\frac{\log a(n)}n\longrightarrow\lambda=r\log2.
\]

Finally, by (12), \(a(n)>0\) for all \(n\ge1\), and hence
\[
a(n)^{1/n}
=\exp\left(\frac{\log a(n)}n\right).
\]
The exponential function is continuous, so (3) yields
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}a(n)^{1/n}
=e^\lambda
=\exp(r\log2)
=2^r,
\]
where \(r\in(1/2,1)\) satisfies
\[
H(r)=r\log2.
\]
In particular, the limit exists, as required.
